feedback.answered: The next entry comparison is concrete. Node.ProposeConfChange says changes are dropped unless the leader has certainty no prior unapplied configuration change remains; Node.Advance permits acknowledgment while commands are still being applied. Node.run forwards Advance to RawNode.Advance, whose recorded StorageApplyResp advances internal applied. stepLeader tests pendingConfIndex against that internal applied before accepting a new configuration proposal. The captured campaign test expects a follower with unapplied committed configuration to remain follower, but uses lower-level test helpers and does not establish the public Node early-Advance contract. Node.Status supplies a serialized public observation barrier, allowing an experiment without private state assignment.
remaining: Execute the prepared Node caller-policy comparison using actual committed configuration producers: defer activation without Advance, defer activation with early Advance, and activate before Advance.
Permission for early Advance on a batch containing a configuration entry remains a semantic premise; preserve observed policy effects even if general responsibility cannot be attributed.
feedback.rationale: A three-policy Node experiment can distinguish whether Advance, rather than ApplyConfChange, releases the pending-change guard. Using the high-level Node API avoids importing RawNode completion duties into a different entry contract. This is a new discriminator, not a reopening of the reviewed asynchronous check.

question.importance: A follower append acknowledgment is consumed as qualified support by the leader. An overly broad overlap permission could expose acknowledgment before the corresponding durable write. This is a caller-contract applicability question at A6/A7 supporting A1, not a demonstrated loss of consensus safety.
